title: What a reading becomes
summary: One telemetry message is stored in one transaction. A good reading becomes a row in observations, any other reading a row in diagnostics, and latest keeps one current row per parameter. The top row decides whether anything is stored at all; the rows below are the tables.

boxes.label: Mapped reading
boxes.detail: received_at is when the runtime got the packet. observed_at is the source's own timestamp when it sent one. timestamp_source says which was used: receipt, source, corrected_future (a source clock more than five minutes ahead is replaced by receipt time) or derived for a calculated reading. Quality is good or invalid.

boxes.label: Generation fence
boxes.detail: The transaction first locks the device's row for share and checks the message's organization, configuration and applied generation against it. No match, or no readings, commits nothing.

boxes.label: Message ledger
boxes.detail: The committed event is inserted with ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING. If the row already exists, this message was stored before and the transaction ends. Published rows are kept at least eight days, longer than the seven days JetStream can redeliver.

boxes.label: For each reading
boxes.detail: The whole reading is stored as JSON beside the columns used to find it. All of a message's inserts are sent to the database as one batch, in order, so a message costs the same few round trips whether it has one reading or fifty. Every row actually inserted is counted, whichever table it went to.

boxes.label: Re-sent sample check
boxes.detail: A device that reconnects re-sends buffered samples under a new message ID, so the ledger cannot catch them. A source-timestamped reading is skipped when the parameter already has an observation with the same observed time and value. Readings stamped at receipt are never compared. The check is planned with the reading's own time, so it looks only at the chunks that can hold a match, however long the retention.

boxes.label: Nothing stored
boxes.detail: A stale generation and a duplicate delivery both return without an error, so the message is not retried. Callers must not read success as stored.

boxes.label: usage_data_points
boxes.detail: The count of inserted observation and diagnostic rows is added to the organization's bucket for the current UTC hour, in the same transaction. A duplicate message or a skipped sample adds nothing.

boxes.label: diagnostics
boxes.detail: One row per message and parameter, with a null value and the reason. Rows expire with the organization's retention. No query endpoint reads this table today; the diagnostic people see comes from latest.

boxes.label: observations
boxes.detail: Good readings only. The primary key is message, parameter and received_at, so the same message cannot insert twice. Chunks follow receipt time, which keeps inserts in the newest chunk. Raw records are read in receipt order; charts, state timelines and counter increases use the observed-time index.

boxes.label: latest
boxes.detail: Keyed by device, configuration and parameter, and replaced only by a reading received later. A good reading replaces the row. Any other reading keeps the stored value and observed time, takes the new quality and diagnostic, and records last_valid_received_at. Historical readings never touch it.

boxes.label: Compressed chunks
boxes.detail: A TimescaleDB policy compresses observation chunks older than two days, segmented by organization, device and parameter and ordered by observed time, newest first. The schema notes about 1 KB a reading before and about 55 bytes after. A backlog older than two days inserts into compressed chunks, which is slower.

steps.text: A message carries readings with a quality, the time the source measured them and the time the runtime received them. Storing starts by checking the device still runs that configuration and generation.
If the configuration was replaced or the device deactivated meanwhile, the transaction commits nothing.
Otherwise the message ID goes into the ledger. A redelivered message is already there, so it also ends here.
A new message continues: each reading is stored by its quality, and the statements for all of them travel to the database together.
A good reading with a source timestamp is first compared with what is stored for the same parameter, observed time and value.
A sample the device re-sent after reconnecting matches, and is not stored or counted again.
Everything else becomes a row in observations, in the one-day chunk for its receipt time.
A reading that failed conversion or validation goes to diagnostics with the reason instead.
A good live reading replaces the parameter's latest row. A historical reading is history only and leaves latest alone.
A failed reading marks the latest row with its quality and diagnostic but keeps the last valid value and when it was received.
The rows inserted are added to the organization's usage bucket for the hour, before the transaction commits.
Two days later TimescaleDB compresses the chunk. Reads and retention deletes still work on it.
